segments.text: YouTube says that in twenty twenty-four, {h}over half of its partner channels earning five figures also made money from something other than ads.
What changes from one stream to the next is {d}who takes a cut of each dollar.
Start with ads. On long videos, YouTube pays you {a}fifty-five cents of every ad dollar. On {s}Shorts, you keep forty-five percent of your share of the pool.
A sponsorship skips the platform. {b}The brand pays you directly, and YouTube takes no share of the fee.
That's why it's the big one. In a NeoReach survey of over three thousand creators, {n}forty-nine percent said brand deals bring in most of their money.
Affiliate links flip the split. You earn a slice of someone else's sale. Amazon pays {r}one to ten percent, depending on the category. On a hundred-dollar pair of headphones, {h}that's three dollars.
Your own product {f}flips it back. Sell a ten-dollar guide on Gumroad, and the fee is ten percent plus fifty cents. {p}You keep eight fifty, before any card fees.
Memberships pay you every month. {y}YouTube channel memberships keep thirty percent. {pt}Patreon charges new creators ten percent, plus payment processing.
So the platform's cut runs from {r1}about half on ads, to {r2}ten to thirty percent on memberships, to {r3}ten percent plus fifty cents on your own product, to {r4}nothing on a sponsor.
Ads only need views. The rest need people who'll pay you directly. Keep the ads running, and build one of these next to them.

_note: No prompt: the backend prepends it to each segment and Gemini flash-lite reads it aloud. Same voice and model as best-times.
